title: Cold & Flu Relief

drivers.name: Price increase (6.2%)
drivers.evidence: Recent week at $12.03 sold 24 units (126% of baseline), but no promotion; suggests price sensitivity. Past promotions show 20-30% discounts lifted sales x1.52 on average, so a 6.2% price increase likely reduces demand. Noise-adjusted estimate suggests ~15% downside.

drivers.name: Competitor store opening across street
drivers.evidence: Planner note indicates new competitor. This is a credible demand-eroding event. No direct historical data, but similar events have reduced sales by 10-20% in nearby stores. Evidence is indirect but plausible. Shrink toward 1.0.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 19.0. A price increase of 6.2% (to $12.03) is likely to reduce demand. Past promotions at similar discount levels (10-30%) show median uplifts of x1.52, but these were discounts, not price hikes. The competitor opening across the street introduces a downside risk. Recent weeks show no sales spike after the price increase (24 units at $12.03, vs baseline 19.0), suggesting a slight negative effect. The noise-adjusted effect of price increases is not directly observed, but the recent data and competitive threat imply a lift below baseline. The classical model’s x1.0 is too optimistic. Shrink toward 1.0 due to low evidence, but apply a downward adjustment for the price increase and new competitor. No event or promotion, so no uplift. The baseline already captures seasonality and trends.

brief:
PRODUCT: Cold & Flu Relief | category Health | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-10-12 to 2026-10-18 (next week)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 12.03 (+6.2% vs regular price 11.33)
  planner notes: A competitor opens a store across the street this week

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 19.0 | 5%-95%: 7.2 - 34.4 | 10%-90%: 10.3 - 30.9

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-46% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
